\chapter{Ha + Y --- The Fossil in a Three-Letter Word}
\label{ch:hay-etymology}
\hlchaptermodality{186}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what hay is made of and name the French phrase built from the same pieces.}

Complete ES-C54-ha-mas-y: name the two pieces, say where else the y appears, and name the French equivalent.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ha + y]{ha + y — the fossil in a three-letter word}

\label{lesson:ES-C54-ha-mas-y}



\begin{quote}
\emph{Hay} looks like nothing. Say the \emph{haber} form for he/she. (\emph{Ha}.) Now look at \emph{hay} again with that in mind.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Hay} is two words fused:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{ha} + \textbf{y}
\end{quote}

The \emph{ha} you already hold: it is \emph{haber}, third person. The \textbf{y} is the interesting half. It is Latin \textbf{ibi}, meaning \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}there\textquotedblright{}} — and Spanish otherwise \textbf{lost that word completely.}

There is no \emph{y} meaning \textquotedblleft{}there\textquotedblright{} anywhere else in modern Spanish. It survives in exactly one place, welded to the front of a verb, because words that get glued to something else stop being available to be replaced. \emph{Hay} is a museum case with one object in it.

So the literal reading is: \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}it has there.\textquotedblright{}} Which is a strange way to say something exists, until you notice that the neighbours do the same:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{French: \emph{il y a}} — \textquotedblleft{}it there has.\textquotedblright{} Same \emph{haber} verb, same \emph{ibi}, same order, three words instead of one. French kept its \emph{y} separate, so its fossil is still visible on the surface.
  \item \textbf{English: \emph{there is}} — which also starts with a place-word doing a job that has nothing to do with place. Nobody is pointing anywhere when they say \emph{there is a problem}.
\end{itemize}

Three languages, three different verbs, and all of them reached for a word meaning \textbf{\textquotedblleft{}there\textquotedblright{}} to announce that something exists. That is not borrowing; it is the same instinct arriving three times.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ha\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}hay\textquotedblright{} — hear the extra piece
  \item \textquotedblleft{}hay\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}il y a\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}there is\textquotedblright{} — three languages, one instinct
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{hay} made of? (\emph{\textbf{Ha}} + \emph{\textbf{y}}.) What does the \emph{y} mean, and where else is it? (\textbf{\textquotedblleft{}There\textquotedblright{}} — and \textbf{nowhere else} in Spanish.) What did French do with the same pieces? (Kept them apart: \emph{\textbf{il y a}}.) Next: \emph{hay} with a verb after it.
\end{tcolorbox}
